# Precision, Effect Size and Clinically Important Difference {#sec-precision-effect-size}

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple" title="Learning objectives"}
- Separate clinical importance from statistical detectability.
- Specify effect units before calculating sample size.
:::

## The idea

Absolute precision describes the tolerated uncertainty in an estimated quantity. An **effect size** describes the magnitude of a difference or association. For a continuous outcome, the target difference should generally be stated in the outcome’s natural units and justified clinically; a standardised difference may help comparability but cannot replace the original clinical scale.

## When and how to apply it

For binary outcomes, a risk difference of 0.05 means five percentage points, not five percent relative change. The same odds ratio can correspond to different absolute changes at different baseline risks. Define whether a reported difference is clinically meaningful, realistic or both.

## Teaching case 1 — baseline draft

::: {.callout-tip appearance="simple" title="Clinical scenario / initial worked example"}
A researcher selects a 5-mmHg systolic blood pressure difference, while another chooses 10 mmHg. With the same SD, which requires a larger sample?
:::

::: {.callout-warning appearance="simple" title="Common error"}
Do not choose an unrealistically large effect just to make the sample size affordable.
:::
